summary: Defines how iSCSI hosts, devices, and management services use the Service Location Protocol (SLP), with SLP service type templates describing their services, so iSCSI targets and name servers can be found.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4018 shows how an iSCSI host finds the storage it should connect to. Storage targets advertise themselves with the Service Location Protocol, listing the names, addresses and access rules that an initiator can search against before it logs in.

questions: how do iscsi initiators discover targets
what is the iscsi default tcp port
subtitle: How an iSCSI host finds storage targets and management servers with the Service Location Protocol.

tldr.problem: An iSCSI initiator has to know the address of the storage target it should talk to, and the usual answers are a static list on the initiator or a list of targets fetched from a known address. Both need configuration on every host.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SLP service types that iSCSI targets and storage management servers register, the attributes that describe them, and the queries an initiator can use to find the targets it is allowed to log in to.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4018 is a Proposed Standard from April 2005 and has been updated by RFC 7146.

today: RFC 4018 is a Proposed Standard from April 2005 and has been updated by RFC 7146. Its service type templates remain the registered way for iSCSI targets and storage management servers to advertise themselves for discovery.

sections.title: Why SLP for iSCSI
sections.content:
iSCSI, defined in RFC 3720, transports SCSI commands, data and status across an IP network. It is connection-oriented and is currently defined over TCP. It uses a client and server relationship: the client end is an initiator, which sends SCSI commands, and the server end is a target, which receives and executes them.

There are several ways for an initiator to find the targets it should connect to, and two of them need no SLP at all. Each target and its address can be configured statically on the initiator, or each address that provides targets can be configured on the initiator, and iSCSI then offers a mechanism to query that address for a list of targets. Both are defined in the iSCSI naming and discovery requirements.

Each of those needs a little configuration on every initiator. Being able to discover targets and name services without configuring initiators is a desirable feature, and the Service Location Protocol, an IETF standards track protocol, provides several features that simplify locating iSCSI services. This document describes how SLP can be used in iSCSI environments to discover targets, addresses that provide targets, and storage management servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Today a host has to be told where its storage lives, or be told where to ask. The Service Location Protocol lets the storage advertise itself instead, so a host can find it with a query.

sections.title: The Terms Used
sections.content:
Some definitions are reproduced from the SLP and the related RSIP server documents. A User Agent is a process working on the client's behalf to establish contact with some service; it retrieves service information from the Service Agents or Directory Agents. A Service Agent is a process working on behalf of one or more services to advertise the services and their capabilities. A Directory Agent is a process that collects service advertisements, and there can be only one on a given host. A Scope is a named set of services, typically making up a logical administrative group. A Service Advertisement is a URL, attributes and a lifetime, giving service access information and a capabilities description for a particular service.

On the storage side, an initiator is a logical entity, typically within a host, that sends SCSI commands to targets to be executed, and is usually a device driver. A target is a logical entity, typically within a storage controller or gateway, that receives those commands and executes them; a target includes one or more Logical Units, each of which is a SCSI device such as a disk or a tape drive. An iSCSI Name is a UTF-8 character string that serves as a unique identifier for iSCSI initiators and targets.

An iSCSI Client is a logical entity, typically a host, that includes at least one initiator, and an iSCSI Server is a logical entity, typically a storage controller or gateway, that includes at least one target. A Storage Management Server is an addressable entity that provides management services that benefit an iSCSI environment; the term is generic and does not indicate a specific protocol or service.
sections.plainLanguage: Three SLP roles again: the service agent advertises, the user agent asks, the directory agent collects. On the storage side, the initiator sends commands and the target executes them, and each has a unique iSCSI name.

sections.title: Discovering iSCSI Targets
sections.content:
An iSCSI client includes at least one initiator and an SLP user agent. An iSCSI server includes at least one target and an SLP service agent. Some entities, such as extended copy engines, include both initiators and targets, and so both a service agent for their targets and a user agent for their initiators.

Each target and initiator has a unique iSCSI name, and that name is the same whatever path the target is discovered and accessed over. An iSCSI target URL consists of the fully qualified host name or IP address, the TCP port the target listens on, and the iSCSI name. A server must register each of its individual targets at each of its network addresses, so a target with two addresses has two service URLs, unless a single service URL used a DNS host name that mapped to both.

The server constructs a service advertisement of the type service:iscsi:target for each service URL it wishes to register, with a lifetime and the other attributes defined in the service template. In the RFC's example, a server listening on TCP port 3260 at two addresses registers six URLs: 192.0.2.131:3260/one, 192.0.2.131:3260/two, 192.0.2.131:3260/three, 192.0.2.3:3260/one, 192.0.2.3:3260/two and 192.0.2.3:3260/three.

The rest of the procedure is the one used by any SLP client and server pair. If a directory agent is found, the service agent registers the advertisement with it; whether or not a directory agent is found, the service agent keeps the advertisement itself and answers multicast user agent queries directly. When the initiator needs contact information for a target, the user agent either contacts the directory agent by unicast or the service agent by multicast, and includes a query based on the attributes to say what characteristics the target must have. A user agent configured with the address of a service agent may avoid multicast entirely and contact it by unicast. Once the user agent has the host name or address of the server, the port number and the target name, it can begin the normal iSCSI login.

Because the information in the target template may exceed common network datagram sizes, the SLP implementation for both user agents and service agents that support the template must implement SLP over TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each target is registered once per address, with a URL that names the address, the port and the iSCSI name. The initiator asks for the targets it needs, and once it has the address, the port and the name, it logs in as usual.

sections.title: Matching Targets by Initiator Credentials
sections.content:
To be allowed access to a target, an initiator must be authenticated, and the target may require it to produce one or more of an iSCSI initiator name, an IP address, a CHAP, SRP or Kerberos credential, or any combination of these.

Most targets allow access to only one or two initiators. In the ideal discovery scenario, an initiator would send an SLP request and receive responses only for targets to which it is guaranteed a successful login. To reach that, the target template carries three attributes, each holding a list of values. auth-name lists the initiator names allowed to access the target, or the value 'any' when no specific name is required. auth-addr lists the host names and IP addresses that will be allowed access, or 'any'. auth-cred lists credentials of the form method/identifier, such as CHAP or SRP with a user name, that will be allowed access, provided the initiator can produce the right password or other verifier during login; the value 'any' means no specific credential is required.

When a target allows access to several host identities, more than one combination of these attributes has to be allowed, and in some cases the whole set of valid combinations cannot be expressed in a single registered service URL. If a target can be addressed by one name with one credential, or by a second name with a second credential, listing all the names and all the credentials together would allow either name with either credential. So a target and address have to be registered under more than one service URL, one for each identity, and because service URLs must be unique, the URL carries an additional opaque string that defines the identity. That string appears after the iSCSI name in the URL and is separated by a slash, and each registered tuple of target address, target name and initiator identity can then carry its own set of attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A target can say in advance who may log in to it: by name, by address, and by credential. An initiator can search on those rules and get back only the targets it will be allowed into.

sections.title: Discovery Without Multicast
sections.content:
In some networks multicast is unavailable or not allowed for discovery. These include public or service-provider networks placed between an iSCSI client and a server, which are probably most common between two iSCSI gateways, one at a storage service provider site and one at a customer site.

In such networks, an initiator may have the addresses of one or more service agents configured, instead of or in addition to its directory agent configuration. The initiator then makes unicast SLP service requests directly to those service agents, without using multicast to find them first. The RFC notes that this is well within the scope of the current SLP protocol, and that the main consequence for implementers is that an initiator configured to make direct unicast requests to a service agent has to add this to the SLP API, if it follows the service location API defined in RFC 2614.
sections.plainLanguage: Where a network blocks multicast, the host can be given the address of the advertising agent and ask it directly, with no group traffic on the wire.

sections.title: Discovering Storage Management Services
sections.content:
Storage management servers can be built to manage and control access to targets in a variety of ways, and can provide extended services beyond discovery, such as storage allocation and management. None of those services are defined here; the intent is to allow them to be discovered by both clients and servers, alongside the target discovery already described.

The storage management server would use its own protocol to provide capabilities to iSCSI clients and servers, and both of those can use SLP to discover it. The model differs from target discovery: when a target was being discovered, the iSCSI server implemented a service agent to be found by the initiator's user agent. In the storage management server model, the iSCSI clients and servers both implement user agents, and the management server implements the service agent.

A storage management server's URL holds the domain name or IP address and the TCP or UDP port number, and nothing else is required. The server constructs a service advertisement of the type service:iscsi:sms for each of the addresses at which it appears, with the URL, a lifetime and the other attributes in the service template. The discovery procedure is then the same as for targets, except that both initiators and targets are normally clients of the storage management service.

A target that supports a storage management service implements a user agent in addition to the service agent. Alternatively, a target may implement only the user agent and let the storage management service advertise its targets, by the management service providing a service agent and registering the appropriate service:iscsi:target registrations on the target's behalf, so that the target device does not advertise its own targets. This has no impact on the initiator, and it means the initiator's discovery of targets stays fully interoperable regardless of which storage management service is used, whether one is used at all, and whether the registrations come from the target or from the management service.
sections.plainLanguage: A management server is found the same way, but the roles are reversed: the storage side advertises the management server, and the hosts and storage both ask for it. A management server may also advertise the targets on the storage's behalf.

sections.title: The Service Type Templates
sections.content:
Three templates are provided: an iSCSI target template, a management service template, and an abstract template to encapsulate the two. All three have template version 1.0.

The abstract template defines the service service:iscsi, used as a top-level service to encapsulate all other iSCSI-related services, with a URL syntax that depends on the concrete service type. The target template defines the service service:iscsi:target, and an entity holding iSCSI targets registers each of them, with each of its addresses, under that type. Its URL syntax is a host and optional port, then a slash, then the iSCSI name, then an optional slash and an identity string. The iSCSI name is required and must be the name of the target being registered, and a device representing several targets must register each target and address combination separately.

The target template defines these attributes: iscsi-name, the iSCSI name of the target, which must match the name in the URL path; portal-group, the iSCSI portal group tag for the address, where addresses sharing the same name and tag can be used within the same iSCSI session; transports, the transport protocols the entity supports, which is TCP today, with SCTP anticipated; mgmt-entity, the name or address of the management interface of the entity holding the target; and alias, a descriptive name for the target. It also defines the three access attributes described earlier, and boot-list, a list of initiator names that may boot from the target, which works like the access list, and which is not registered at all when the target is not bootable.

The management service template defines the service service:iscsi:sms. An entity supporting one or more iSCSI management service protocols may register itself under that type, and clients and servers usually search for them by the protocols they support, with the query (protocols=isns) as the example. Its URL is the URL of the management service. Its attributes are protocols, the list of protocols the name service supports, with no default, transports, which for this service lists TCP and UDP, and server-priority, the priority a client should give this server when choosing between several with the same protocol type. The precedence is protocol-specific: with iSNS, for example, the primary server has the lowest value, which is 0.

On internationalization, SLP allows internationalized strings to be registered and retrieved. Template attributes that are not marked as literal are registered in a localized manner; an English localization must be registered and others may be. Attributes that include non-ASCII characters are encoded with UTF-8.

The three templates have been reviewed and approved by the IESG and registered in IANA's SVRLOC Templates registry, following the process described in RFC 2609.
sections.plainLanguage: Three templates describe what a target, a management server and the family around them look like: how the URL is written and what attributes come with it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The SLPv2 security model provides no confidentiality but does provide a way for user agents to be sure that service advertisements come only from trusted service agents, except that it has no mechanism to authenticate a response that returns no results.

Once a target or management server has been discovered, authentication and authorisation are handled by the iSCSI protocol, or by the management server's own protocol. It is the responsibility of the providers of those services to make sure that an inappropriately advertised or discovered service does not compromise their security.

Without security in SLPv2, false discovery information may be distributed. The primary countermeasure is authentication: where the risk matters, IPsec security associations and iSCSI in-band authentication should be used, so that traffic only flows between endpoints that took part in IKE authentication and iSCSI in-band authentication. An attacker who distributes discovery information claiming to be an iSCSI target will lack the secrets needed to complete those exchanges and so will be prevented from sending or receiving iSCSI traffic falsely.

A denial of service risk remains, based on repeated use of false discovery information that triggers IKE negotiation. The countermeasures are administrative configuration of each iSCSI target to limit the peers it will talk to, by IP address range or DNS domain, and a negative authentication cache that avoids repeatedly contacting a target that fails to authenticate. These three measures must be implemented.

The auth-name, auth-addr, auth-cred and boot-list attributes are security policy information, and when they are distributed IPsec must be implemented. If IPsec is not implemented, that information must not be distributed via SLPv2 and must not be used if it is discovered that way.

For the implementation, security for SLPv2 in an IP storage environment is specified in RFC 3723. IPsec is mandatory to implement for the block storage clients and servers, so all of them, including those invoking SLP, can be assumed to support it. SLP servers cannot be assumed to implement IPsec, because standard SLP has no such requirement, and in particular a directory agent may run on a machine that runs no block storage protocol. IPsec should be implemented for SLPv2, including ESP with a non-null transform to give both authentication and confidentiality. Because the storage services have their own authentication capabilities once located, SLPv2 authentication is optional to implement and use.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding a target proves nothing, so the iSCSI login still authenticates the peer. The access rules published in discovery are themselves sensitive, and the RFC says they must not travel without IPsec.

messages.label: Service registration
messages.note: The service agent registers a service:iscsi:target advertisement for each address.

messages.label: Service request
messages.note: A query on the attributes says what kind of target is wanted.

messages.label: Service reply
messages.note: Returns the URLs of the matching targets, with the port and the iSCSI name.

messages.label: iSCSI login
messages.note: The normal login starts from the address, port and target name found.

viz.caption: THE THREE ACCESS ATTRIBUTES OF THE TARGET TEMPLATE

items.title: auth-name
items.text: The initiator names allowed to reach the target, or the value any.

items.title: auth-addr
items.text: The host names and IP addresses allowed to reach the target, or the value any.

items.title: auth-cred
items.text: Credentials of the form method/identifier, such as chap or srp with a user name.
